# Cold open

<!-- scene: co_s01 -->
Throw a stick onto a wooden floor. [pause 0.5s] Then another, and another. [pause 1.0s] Count how often one lands across a crack between the boards, and from that count alone, you can work out *pi*. [pause 2.0s] There is no circle anywhere on this floor. [pause 0.6s] So where is it hiding?

> [pause 2.5]

# Intro

<!-- scene: in_s01 -->
Most of us met math as a list of chores. [pause 0.4s] Add these. [pause 0.2s] Solve for x. [pause 0.2s] Show your work. [pause 1.0s] Mathematicians mean something else by the word. [pause 0.4s] They mean the study of patterns. [pause 0.4s] A ripple on a pond, the rim of a wheel and the face of a clock all share one shape. [pause 0.3s] Math studies that shape stripped down, until only the pattern is left.

> [pause 2]

<!-- scene: in_s02 -->
In school, math arrives one piece at a time. [pause 0.3s] A year of algebra, a year of geometry, a little statistics near the end. [pause 0.8s] Each piece makes sense on its own, but nobody shows how they fit together. [pause 0.6s] It's like learning a city one street at a time, without ever seeing the map. [pause 0.8s] With the map, a new idea stops being a stray fact. [pause 0.3s] It becomes a place you can find again, next to things you already know.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: in_s03 -->
And the map is worth seeing, because its pieces are everywhere. [pause 0.4s] Your phone finds you where circles of distance around several satellites meet. [pause 0.6s] A spam filter weighs the odds that a message is junk. [pause 0.6s] Every secure payment leans on the arithmetic of whole numbers. [pause 0.6s] And spacecraft reach other planets because calculus tells us where to aim.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: in_s04 -->
So, the plan. [pause 0.3s] We'll take one circle and look at it through each major branch of math in turn: what it is, how big it is, how it turns, what shape it really has, how it grows, and what it has to do with chance. [pause 1.2s] Each look lights up one part of the map.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: in_s05 -->
Before we start, a promise. [pause 0.4s] By the end, you'll see exactly why those sticks on the floor found pi, and why the answer needs every part of this map at once. [pause 0.8s] And one small thing to watch for. [pause 0.3s] Each time we move on, the whole map will turn by the same amount. [pause 0.4s] That turning is math too, and we'll come back to it. # Foundations

<!-- scene: ch1_s01 -->
Picture a dog tied to a post. [pause 0.4s] When it pulls the leash tight, it can stand in lots of places, but not just anywhere. [pause 0.6s] Every spot it can reach with the leash tight is exactly one leash length from the post. [pause 1.0s] Gather up all of those spots, and they make a circle. [pause 0.8s] That shift, from a shape we recognize to a rule we can check, is the first idea of *foundations*.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch1_s02 -->
Mathematicians call a collection like this a *set*. [pause 0.4s] A set is defined by a rule, and the rule decides, for every possible point, whether it's in or out. [pause 0.8s] There's no partly in. [pause 0.6s] Change the rule, and you change the set. [pause 0.3s] Let the leash go slack, and the set fills in to a whole disk. [pause 1.0s] The circle is only the points that are *exactly* one leash length away.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch1_s03 -->
To make the rule exact, put the post at the center of a grid. [pause 0.4s] Every point on the circle is the corner of a right triangle whose longest side is the leash. [pause 0.3s] Pythagoras turns *one leash length away* into a test you can run on any point's coordinates. [pause 1.2s] Wrap that test in braces, and the circle is written as a set. [pause 0.5s] Georg Cantor started the study of sets in the eighteen seventies, and sets became the ground floor of mathematics. [pause 0.6s] A point belongs to this one *if and only if* it passes the test. [pause 0.4s] The promise runs in both directions.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch1_s04 -->
Try it with a leash five units long. [pause 0.3s] Which of these points can the dog reach with the leash tight? [pause 2.0s] The first passes the test exactly, so it sits on the circle. [pause 0.8s] The second comes up short, so it's inside. [pause 0.5s] The third overshoots: outside. [pause 1.0s] One test sorts every point in the plane into exactly one of three sets, with nothing left over and nothing counted twice.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch1_s05 -->
That two-way promise matters. [pause 0.5s] Roll a circle under a flat board, and the board glides along at a constant height. [pause 0.6s] So you might guess the reverse: anything that rolls that smoothly must be a circle. [pause 1.2s] It doesn't have to be. [pause 0.5s] This rounded triangle, built from three arcs, keeps the board just as level. [pause 1.0s] The British fifty pence coin uses the same trick with seven sides, so vending machines can measure its width like a circle's. [pause 1.0s] A statement and its reverse are different claims, and logic is the habit of checking both.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch1_s06 -->
Anyone who shops online uses this. [pause 0.3s] Filter for shoes that are red *and* in your size, and the shop returns the overlap of two sets. [pause 0.5s] Ask for red *or* your size, and it returns everything in either one. [pause 1.0s] Underneath all of math sit definitions like these: rules that say exactly what is in and what is out. [pause 0.8s] Everything else is built on top.

> [pause 3]

# Quantity

<!-- scene: ch2_s01 -->
How big is a circle? [pause 0.4s] Take a wheel exactly one unit across, paint a dot on its rim, and roll it along a number line for one full turn. [pause 0.3s] Where will the dot touch down? [pause 2.0s] Just past three. [pause 0.6s] That length is the distance around the wheel, and it has a name: *pi*. [pause 0.8s] Every circle, from a coin to a Ferris wheel, measures pi times its own width all the way around.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch2_s02 -->
So pi is a little more than three. [pause 0.3s] You'd expect some fraction to land on it exactly, if we just find the right one. [pause 0.8s] More than two thousand years ago, Archimedes trapped pi between two fractions by drawing polygons with ninety-six sides. [pause 0.5s] The upper one, twenty-two sevenths, is still used in schools. [pause 0.6s] Around the year four eighty, Zu Chongzhi in China found three hundred fifty-five over one hundred thirteen, right to six decimal places. [pause 0.8s] Zoom in on either one, and there is still a gap.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch2_s03 -->
Each kind of number answers a need. [pause 0.3s] Counting gives the whole numbers. [pause 0.3s] Owing gives the negatives. [pause 0.3s] Sharing a pizza gives fractions, which mathematicians call *rational* numbers. [pause 0.8s] And fractions are packed tight: between any two sits another, halfway between, and another between those, without end. [pause 1.0s] It looks as if they leave no room for anything else.

> [pause 0.8]

<!-- scene: ch2_s04 -->
Fit a square inside a circle of radius one. [pause 0.4s] Its diagonal runs straight across the circle, so it's two units long, and Pythagoras makes each side the square root of two. [pause 0.8s] Is that length a fraction? [pause 1.5s] Suppose it is, in lowest terms. [pause 0.4s] Squaring gives an equation in whole numbers, and it forces the top number to be even. [pause 0.6s] Feed that back in, and the bottom number must be even too. [pause 0.8s] But a fraction in lowest terms can't have both numbers even. [pause 0.6s] The assumption fails, so the square root of two is not a fraction. [pause 0.5s] Numbers like this are called *irrational*.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch2_s05 -->
In seventeen sixty-one, Johann Lambert proved that pi is irrational too, so its decimals never fall into a repeating loop. [pause 0.8s] In practice, we never need them all. [pause 0.3s] Navigators at NASA use fifteen decimal places to steer spacecraft between planets. [pause 0.6s] Forty places would give the distance around the visible universe to within the width of an atom.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch2_s06 -->
Numbers come in kinds, and even a simple circle holds lengths that no fraction can name. [pause 0.8s] And notice how we showed it: assume the opposite, follow the rules, and arrive at something impossible. [pause 0.5s] That move comes straight from foundations.

> [pause 3]

# Structure

<!-- scene: ch3_s01 -->
Turn a square a little, and you can tell it moved. [pause 0.5s] Turn it a quarter of the way around, and it looks exactly as it did before. [pause 0.8s] Now turn the circle. [pause 0.3s] Turn it by any amount at all, and nothing seems to change. [pause 1.0s] A move that leaves a shape looking the same is called a *symmetry*. [pause 0.4s] The square has four turning symmetries. [pause 0.3s] The circle has one for every angle.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch3_s02 -->
Mathematicians study the moves themselves. [pause 0.4s] Think of the dial on a combination lock. [pause 0.3s] Turn it thirty degrees, then forty-five more, and together that's one turn of seventy-five. [pause 0.6s] Any turn can be undone by turning back, and leaving the dial alone counts as a turn of zero. [pause 1.0s] Moves you can combine and undo, including the move that does nothing, form what's called a *group*. [pause 0.5s] Groups are one of the basic objects of *algebra*.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch3_s03 -->
Remember how the map turns each time we move on? [pause 0.4s] It's always a sixth of a full circle, and six of those bring it back to the start. [pause 0.8s] Those six turns, counting the one that does nothing, form a group of their own, the *cyclic group of order six*. [pause 0.6s] A snowflake has the same six turns. [pause 0.6s] By the end of this video, the map will have made all six.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch3_s04 -->
Turns can be numbers too. [pause 0.4s] Multiplying by minus one flips the number line around: a half turn. [pause 0.6s] So what would a quarter turn be? [pause 1.2s] Call it *i*. [pause 0.3s] Do it twice, and you've made a half turn, the same as multiplying by minus one. [pause 0.5s] That's all the square root of minus one means: a quarter turn, off the line and into the plane.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch3_s05 -->
Leonhard Euler found a way to write *any* turn as a number. [pause 0.4s] Each one is a power of a single constant, the number e, which we'll meet properly in the chapter on change. [pause 1.0s] As the angle grows, the point sweeps around the circle, with cosine as its shadow along one axis and sine along the other. [pause 0.8s] Keep an eye on e, i and pi. [pause 0.4s] Before the end, all three will meet in one short line.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch3_s06 -->
Turns written this way are easy to combine. [pause 0.3s] Take a turn of sixty degrees and a turn of thirty. [pause 0.3s] What does multiplying them give? [pause 1.5s] Expanding the brackets, the pieces combine, and everything cancels except i: a turn of ninety degrees. [pause 0.8s] Multiplying turns adds their angles. [pause 0.5s] The angle formulas from school trigonometry are hiding inside that one line.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch3_s07 -->
The same idea steers machines. [pause 0.3s] In eighteen forty-three, William Rowan Hamilton found numbers that do for turns in space what i does in the plane, and he carved the rule into a bridge in Dublin. [pause 0.6s] Today these numbers, called quaternions, turn the camera in video games and tell your phone which way is up. [pause 1.0s] For a circle, the moves are turns, and the turns are numbers. [pause 0.8s] Algebra is the study of moves like these.

> [pause 3]

# Space

<!-- scene: ch4_s01 -->
We're halfway around the map, and we still owe you the sticks on the floor. [pause 0.5s] We need a closer look at shape and at change first, and then we'll have everything. [pause 1.0s] So, shape. [pause 0.3s] Think of the circle as a rubber band, and squash it into a square. [pause 1.2s] To a geometer, everything just changed: the curve is gone, and corners appeared. [pause 0.6s] To a topologist, nothing happened at all.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch4_s02 -->
Topology is geometry with the measurements thrown away. [pause 0.4s] Stretching, bending and squashing are allowed, as much as you like. [pause 0.3s] Cutting and gluing are not. [pause 0.8s] So the rubber band can become a triangle, or a wobbly blob, or a star. [pause 0.6s] What it can't become is a figure eight, because that means pinching two points together. [pause 1.0s] To a topologist, every one of these loops is the same circle.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch4_s03 -->
So what does survive a stretch? [pause 0.6s] Holes. [pause 0.4s] Draw a loop on a flat disk, and it can always shrink down to a point. [pause 0.5s] Wrap a loop once around the rubber band, and it snags on the hole, however it's stretched. [pause 0.8s] On the surface of a donut, a loop can snag in two different ways. [pause 1.0s] Loops that can't be shrunk are one of the main ways topologists tell shapes apart.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch4_s04 -->
Euler found an even simpler test. [pause 0.3s] Build a shape from corners, edges and faces, add up the corners and faces, and take away the edges. [pause 0.8s] Any loop comes out at zero. [pause 0.4s] Fill it in, and the face makes it one. [pause 0.5s] A cube comes out at two. [pause 0.6s] What about the donut? [pause 1.5s] Zero again. [pause 0.4s] Cut any of these into different pieces, or stretch them however you like, and the count never changes.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch4_s05 -->
That's why people joke that a topologist can't tell a coffee mug from a donut. [pause 0.5s] Squash the mug down into its handle, and what's left is a ring with one hole. [pause 1.2s] Both count out at zero. [pause 0.4s] To topology they're the same shape. [pause 0.8s] Biologists use the same way of thinking to follow how long strands of DNA tangle and untangle inside a cell.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch4_s06 -->
If you've ridden a subway, you've used this idea. [pause 0.3s] In nineteen thirty-three, Harry Beck redrew the map of the London Underground with straight lines and evenly spaced stops. [pause 0.6s] Distances were wrong everywhere, but which stops connect to which stayed exactly right. [pause 0.8s] Riders found it far easier to use, and transit maps around the world have copied the idea ever since.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch4_s07 -->
A circle and a square disagree on every measurement, and agree on everything that survives a stretch. [pause 0.8s] Even with every length thrown away, we still ended up counting. [pause 0.6s] Next, the lengths come back, because the circle is about to grow.

> [pause 3]

# Change

<!-- scene: ch5_s01 -->
Drop a stone into still water. [pause 1.0s] The ripple spreads as a circle, and its radius grows at a steady pace. [pause 0.6s] You'd expect the area inside to grow steadily too. [pause 1.0s] It doesn't. [pause 0.3s] Every second, the ripple sweeps over more new water than the second before. [pause 0.8s] Asking how fast something is changing, at a single instant, is the question behind *calculus*.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch5_s02 -->
A car's speedometer answers that kind of question. [pause 0.4s] It doesn't show your average over the trip, but how fast you're going right now. [pause 0.8s] To make right now precise, zoom in on a smooth curve until it looks like a straight line. [pause 0.6s] The steepness of that line is the *derivative*: the rate of change at a single point. [pause 1.0s] Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz built calculus on this idea in the late sixteen hundreds.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch5_s03 -->
One curve has a special property: at every point, its steepness matches its height. [pause 0.8s] It grows the way savings do when interest keeps compounding: the more there is, the faster it grows. [pause 0.6s] Its heights are powers of one particular number, about two point seven one eight, called *e*. [pause 1.0s] This is the same e that Euler used to describe turns.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch5_s04 -->
Back to the circle. [pause 0.3s] Grow its radius by a tiny amount, and the new area is a thin ring around the edge. [pause 0.6s] Cut the ring and unroll it, and it's almost a rectangle: as long as the circumference, and as thick as the nudge. [pause 1.0s] So the area grows at a rate equal to the length of the edge. [pause 0.6s] The derivative of the circle's area is its circumference.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch5_s05 -->
Try it on a pizza ten centimeters in radius. [pause 0.3s] Stretch the dough until the radius grows by one millimeter. [pause 0.3s] How much more pizza is that? [pause 1.5s] The edge times the nudge says about six point two eight square centimeters. [pause 0.6s] Working it out exactly gives six point three one. [pause 0.8s] The small difference is there because the ring's outer edge is a little longer than its inner edge. [pause 0.5s] Make the nudge ten times smaller, and the difference gets a hundred times smaller.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch5_s06 -->
Calculus also runs the other way. [pause 0.4s] Peel a whole disk into thin rings, unroll each one, and stack them, smallest on top. [pause 1.0s] They make a triangle as tall as the radius, with the circumference as its base. [pause 0.6s] Its area works out to exactly the area of the circle. [pause 0.8s] Adding up infinitely many thin pieces is called *integration*, and it undoes the derivative. [pause 0.6s] Archimedes proved the circle matches this triangle more than two thousand years ago.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch5_s07 -->
Every weather forecast is built this way: small changes in air and water, worked out step by step and added up. [pause 1.0s] For a circle, the rate at which its area grows is its own edge. [pause 0.8s] Change is measured by derivatives and added up by integrals.

# Uncertainty

<!-- scene: ch6_s01 -->
Back to the floor and the sticks, as promised. [pause 0.8s] One throw is unpredictable. [pause 0.3s] Will this stick cross a crack? [pause 0.6s] There's no way to know, just as there's no way to call a single coin flip. [pause 0.8s] But many throws together follow a pattern, and that pattern is the subject of *probability*.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch6_s02 -->
Flip a coin again and again, and keep track of the share of heads. [pause 0.6s] Early on, it jumps around. [pause 0.4s] After a thousand flips it hugs one half, and the longer it runs, the closer it stays. [pause 1.0s] Jacob Bernoulli proved this in a book published in seventeen thirteen: averages of many random events settle down. [pause 0.6s] One flip tells you nothing. [pause 0.3s] A million flips land within a whisker of one half.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch6_s03 -->
Make the sticks exactly as long as the boards are wide. [pause 0.4s] Then describe each throw with two numbers: how far the middle of the stick lands from the nearest crack, and the angle it makes with the boards. [pause 0.8s] Every throw becomes a dot in a rectangle of possibilities, and every dot is equally likely. [pause 0.6s] The stick crosses a crack exactly when its dot falls under this curve, one arch of a sine wave. [pause 0.8s] So what share of throws should cross?

> [pause 2.5]

<!-- scene: ch6_s04 -->
The share of sticks that cross is the share of the rectangle under the arch. [pause 0.5s] Calculus gives the area under one arch of a sine wave: exactly two. [pause 0.6s] The rectangle is a half turn wide, so its area is pi. [pause 1.0s] So the crossing share is two over pi, about sixty-four percent. [pause 1.0s] And that's where the circle was hiding: in the angle. [pause 0.4s] Every direction a stick can point lies on a circle, and pi is what it takes to go halfway around.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch6_s05 -->
The French naturalist Buffon worked this out in the seventeen hundreds. [pause 0.6s] In nineteen-oh-one, Mario Lazzarini reported three thousand four hundred and eight throws that gave pi to six decimal places. [pause 0.8s] That's suspiciously good. [pause 0.4s] A random estimate improves slowly: each extra correct digit takes about a hundred times more throws. [pause 0.6s] His answer was exactly Zu Chongzhi's fraction, and his numbers suggest he chose when to stop.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch6_s06 -->
Measuring things with random samples is now a standard tool, called the *Monte Carlo* method, named in the nineteen forties after the famous casino. [pause 0.8s] The animated films you watch are lit this way: a computer follows millions of random paths of light and averages them. [pause 0.8s] And when a medical trial reports that a treatment works, statistics is what tells us whether the result could just be luck.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch6_s07 -->
Many random events add up to numbers you can trust, and sometimes those numbers are old friends, like pi. [pause 0.8s] And to get there, the sticks needed every branch we've seen. [pause 0.5s] So let's see how the branches fit together.

Six turns later, the map is right back where it started, just as the group of turns promised. [pause 1.0s] And the branches were never really separate. [pause 0.4s] Statistics runs on calculus. [pause 0.3s] The secure messages on your phone run on the algebra of whole numbers. [pause 0.3s] Physics runs on symmetry. [pause 0.6s] And under every one of them sit the definitions we started with.

Back in the chapter on structure, we promised that e, i and pi would meet. [pause 0.6s] Turn by pi, a half turn, and you land on minus one. [pause 0.8s] Written as an equation, that's Euler's identity. [pause 1.2s] The e comes from change. [pause 0.3s] The i comes from turning. [pause 0.3s] Pi comes from the circle, and one and zero are where counting starts. [pause 1.0s] One short line, touching almost every part of the map.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch7_s03 -->
And the sticks on the floor needed all of it. [pause 0.6s] Definitions said exactly what counts as a crossing. [pause 0.4s] Symmetry said every angle is equally likely. [pause 0.4s] Geometry turned each throw into a dot in a rectangle. [pause 0.4s] Calculus measured the area under the arch. [pause 0.4s] Probability turned that area into a share of throws. [pause 0.4s] And out came pi, a number no fraction can reach. [pause 1.2s] No single branch could have found it alone.

> [pause 1.2]

Mathematicians lean on these connections all the time. [pause 0.4s] In nineteen ninety-four, Andrew Wiles settled a question about whole numbers that had stood open for more than three hundred and fifty years, using tools from geometry and algebra. [pause 1.0s] Every lens saw something true, and each needed the others.

<!-- scene: out_s01 -->
